You talk about feelings in the past with correct sequence of tenses: temevo che fosse, speravo che venisse, mi dispiaceva che non l’avesse saputo, pensavo che sarebbe venuto, avrei voluto che tu ci fossi; you use a nuanced vocabulary of emotions.
regret (for what you didn’t do / what was lost)
I was afraid you weren’t ready.
I was hoping you’d tell me before Christmas.
I was sorry Aldo never found out.
I would have liked Grandpa to be here.
To use the imperfect subjunctive after verbs of feeling in the past: temevo che fosse, speravo che venisse.
To use the pluperfect subjunctive for an earlier action: mi dispiaceva che non l’avesse saputo.
To express the future in the past with the past conditional: pensavo che sarebbe venuto.
To use “avrei voluto che” + imperfect / pluperfect subjunctive.
To distinguish rimpianto from rimorso, commuoversi from emozionarsi, nostalgia from malinconia.
To describe mixed feelings: felice ma triste, sollevato ma commosso.
On the terrace, on Christmas Eve
Florence, 24 December. After dinner, Pietro and Bianca are left alone on the terrace in via della Chiesa. Pietro has been wanting to tell her something for weeks.
I have to tell you something. I’ve been thinking about it for weeks.
For weeks? I thought you’d never notice.
What you’re about to tell me. I was hoping you’d tell me before the year was over.
At Arcetri I was afraid you liked Andrei.
I told you: not in the way you thought. I was sorry you hadn’t understood.
I wish I’d understood sooner. I’m a bit ashamed.
Don’t be ashamed. I’m in no hurry. But say it now.
I know. Me too. And for once you didn’t ask a single question.
Double SS, stress on “FOS”: FOS-se, FOS-si.
1. Sequence of tenses with the subjunctive (in the past)
When the main verb (of feeling, opinion, wish) is in the past, the subjunctive in the subordinate clause also moves into the past.
Mi dispiace che non l’abbia saputo.
Mi dispiaceva che non l’avesse saputo.
Careful: the future in the past is expressed in Italian with the PAST conditional, not the present: “Pensavo che sarebbe venuto”, not “che verrebbe”. English uses “would come” here.
I’d like you to be here (now)
Avrei voluto che tu ci fossi.
I would have liked you to be there
Avrei voluto che me l’avessi detto.
I wish you had told me
I wish I had understood sooner (same subject)
If the subject is the same, use the infinitive: “Avrei voluto capire” (I… I). If it’s different, “che” + subjunctive: “Avrei voluto che tu capissi” (I… you).
3. The vocabulary of feelings — pairs of nuances
regret for what you didn’t do / what was lost
remorse for what you did wrong
longing for a place, a time
to have one’s heart in one’s mouth
toccare il cielo con un dito
to feel like a fish out of water
to have butterflies in one’s stomach
to breathe a sigh of relief
Real feelings are rarely simple. Italian has structures to describe them together:
Ero felice ma triste allo stesso tempo.
Da una parte ero sollevata, dall’altra mi dispiaceva.
Non so se ridere o piangere.
Provavo un misto di gratitudine e malinconia.
A piece of Graziella’s advice: when you don’t know what you feel, name all the feelings, one after another. One of them will be the true one.
She was glad everyone had come.
He had promised me he would come back.
Regret for something you didn’t do:
Same subject: “I wish I had understood”:
Sulla terrazza, la sera della vigilia di Natale
Che Pietro non se ne sarebbe mai accorto
Che cosa temeva Pietro ad Arcetri?
Che Pietro parlasse prima della fine dell’anno
Che cosa nota Bianca alla fine?
Che Pietro non ha fatto nessuna domanda

Graziella announced it on the first Sunday of December, at the dinner the trattoria gave every year for the people who worked there, just after the Christmas lights had been switched on above via Maggio. Everyone was round the big table: Karl, Matei and Giulia, Marco and Sara, Pietro, Bianca, Viola on Davide’s knees, Guido, who had been invited “as linguistic consultant”, Bellini, and the two waiters who helped on Saturdays. Halfway through dinner, between the ribollita and the stew, Graziella tapped her spoon on her glass. She said she had taken a decision, and had taken it alone, without asking anyone, because some decisions are taken alone. From the first of January she would no longer be the trattoria’s cook. She would retire. The kitchen would pass to Karl. She would keep only two things: the Sunday ribollita and the hug. A silence fell over the room so deep that you could hear the fridge. Karl put down his fork. Pietro felt a lump in his throat. And Viola, the only one able to speak, asked: “But then who hugs the customers on the other days?”

Graziella laughed and said that from then on hugs would be everyone’s job. Then she explained her reasons, one by one, as if she had prepared them for a long time. She said Dr Neri, at her last check-up, had told her that her heart was fine, but wouldn’t stay fine forever if she went on working as before. She said that in fifty-five years in the kitchen she had never seen a sunset from any window but the one above the sink. She said she wanted to watch Viola grow up, and not from behind the counter. She said she wanted to go to Naples in May, for Assunta’s flower, and to Sibiu, at last, to see Ion and Doina’s house. And she said, above all, that she had found someone to leave the kitchen to, and that this was a stroke of luck few people have. She looked at Karl. “I was afraid I wouldn’t find anyone,” she said. “For years I was frightened that when I went, the ribollita would go with me. Instead along came a Maltese man soaked to the skin with ten euros in his pocket.” Karl lowered his eyes to his plate. Pietro saw his shoulders shaking.

There were as many reactions as there were people round the table, and none of them was simple. Marco, who had been asking his mother to slow down for years, breathed a sigh of relief, but straight afterwards was moved, because he understood an era was ending. Matei said he was happy for her but sad for the trattoria, and Giulia elbowed him, because you didn’t say such things in front of Karl. Bellini was silent for a long time, then said that when he retired he had been afraid of feeling useless, and had instead discovered that he finally had time to look at the things he had only restored for forty years. Guido said he couldn’t believe it: Graziella retired was like the Arno without water. Davide said nothing, but drew on his paper napkin a woman with her apron hanging on a nail, and passed it to Graziella, who folded it and put it in her pocket. Pietro, instead, couldn’t speak. He felt a mixture of things he couldn’t put in order: pride, sadness, fear, and a kind of advance regret for something that hadn’t ended yet. Under the table, Bianca took his hand. It was the first time. Neither of them said anything.

Karl spoke last, when everyone had finished. He stood up, as he had on Ferragosto, and said he wasn’t ready. That he could make ribollita, yes, but a trattoria kitchen wasn’t a ribollita: it was a hundred things at once, suppliers, shifts, accounts, difficult customers, evenings when everything went wrong, and he had never done them alone. He said he was afraid of letting her down. That he feared customers would come in on the first of January, not see her behind the counter, and leave. Graziella let him finish. Then she told him something that Pietro wrote word for word in the black notebook that night. “I was afraid too,” she said. “In 1974, when my father left me the kitchen, I was twenty and couldn’t do anything. I thought all the customers would leave. Instead they stayed. Not because I was good. Because my father, before he stepped down, had told everyone he trusted me. And that’s what I’m doing now, in front of everyone: I trust you.”

That night Karl phoned his mother in Marsaxlokk. Pietro found out the next day, because Karl told him in the kitchen while they peeled potatoes, his eyes still puffy. It was eleven at night, and in Malta his mother was already in bed, but she answered on the first ring, the way mothers answer when the phone rings at a strange hour. Karl told her everything: the dinner, the announcement, the kitchen that would become his. His mother was silent for so long that he thought the line had dropped. Then he heard her crying. She told him, in Maltese, that when he left for Rome two years earlier, with a suitcase and an apprentice restorer’s diploma, she had been afraid he would never find his place in the world. That she had hoped one day he would find a home, not a home of walls, but a home of people. And that she would never have imagined that home would be a kitchen in Florence, with an old Florentine lady and a bread soup. “Thank her for me,” said his mother. “Tell her I’ll paint an eye on the kitchen door for her, like on the boats. To protect her.”

The weeks of December passed quickly and strangely. Graziella began teaching Karl the things she had never taught anyone, because they weren’t recipes: they were habits. How to talk to the butcher so he keeps the best cuts aside for you. How to tell from the colour of the sky in the morning how many customers will come for lunch. How to comfort a waiter who has spilled a plate on a customer. How to answer a tourist who asks for a cappuccino after his steak. Which neighbour has no money but doesn’t say so, and has to be fed without making him feel it. Karl took notes in a notebook, and Graziella snatched it out of his hand. “This isn’t written down,” she said. “It’s remembered.” Pietro watched them working together and felt a strange nostalgia, a nostalgia for the present, as if that kitchen, with his grandmother and Karl arguing over the salt, were already a memory. He told Bianca. Bianca explained that in Portuguese there was a word for that feeling, “saudade”, and that in Romanian too, according to Andrei, there was “dor”. Not in Italian. “Then invent one,” said Bianca. Pietro tried for days. He couldn’t.

Viola, on the other hand, took the news in her own way. One evening she asked Graziella what “going into retirement” meant. Graziella explained that it meant stopping work after many years and finally having time to do the things you had never been able to do. Viola thought about it. Then she said she thought retired grandparents slept all day and watched television, like a classmate’s grandfather. Graziella laughed and asked whether she could see her sleeping all day. Viola shook her head, convinced. So Graziella made her an offer. Every Sunday morning, when she made the Sunday ribollita, the only one she had kept, Viola would help her. She would teach her everything, from the beginning: how to cut the black cabbage, why the bread has to be two days old, when to add the salt. And the secret leaf, of course, which Viola already knew. Viola’s eyes widened. She asked whether that meant she would become a cook. Graziella answered that she would become whatever she wanted. But that in life you had to know how to make a ribollita anyway. “Like reading,” she said. “Like hugging.”

Meanwhile there was the other thing, the one Pietro couldn’t tell anyone, not even the black notebook. Since that dinner, since Bianca had taken his hand under the table, he thought of nothing else. He watched her transcribing interviews into the green notebook, explaining a word to Viola, arguing with Davide about slang, and he felt butterflies in his stomach, as the expression he had always found ridiculous put it. But he couldn’t talk to her. Every time he tried, Arcetri came to mind: Bianca and Andrei under the cypresses, the untranslatable words, “dor” and “abbiocco”, and that sentence she had said to him walking down to Porta Romana, “not in the way you think”, which he had never fully understood. He was afraid he had misunderstood. He was afraid that hand under the table had only been a gesture of comfort, the kind you make to a sad friend. And he was afraid, above all, of ruining everything: the friendship, the green notebook, the walks to Arcetri, the evenings transcribing words. He confessed it to Davide one evening at the bar below the workshop. Davide looked at him the way you look at a child who can’t tie his shoes. “You really are a bischero,” he said.

Davide explained, with the patience of a teacher, what everyone except him had understood for months. That Bianca had never had eyes for Andrei. That at Arcetri she talked to Andrei because he was a friend, and nice, and because she wanted to study untranslatable words. That the sentence “not in the way you think” meant exactly the opposite of what Pietro had feared. And that, to top it off, Andrei had a girlfriend in Sibiu, a certain Ioana, who studied violin at the conservatory, and Davide knew because Andrei wrote to him every week for advice on his astronomical drawings. Pietro was speechless. He asked Davide why he hadn’t told him before. Davide shrugged. “I thought you’d notice by yourself,” he said. “You’re the one who asks questions. But on this, funnily enough, you never asked a single one.” Then he patted him on the shoulder, finished his coffee in one gulp and stood up. Before leaving he turned round. “Come on, bischero,” he said. “Christmas is in ten days. Please: don’t make her wait until next year.”

That same evening, to be sure, Pietro wrote to Andrei. He asked him, circling the subject with ridiculous caution, how he was, how things were in Sibiu, whether he had any news. Andrei answered after a minute with a photograph: a blonde girl with a violin under her chin, on the stage of the Sibiu conservatory, and underneath: “Ioana. Christmas concert. Isn’t she beautiful?”. Then a second message: “I thought you knew! I told Davide a month ago. And Bianca too, at Arcetri. I asked her advice on how to write Ioana a love letter in Italian, because Ioana is learning Italian. Bianca helped me with the prepositions.” Pietro reread the message three times. All those conversations under the cypresses, all those untranslatable words, “dor” and “abbiocco”, everything that had tormented him for two months: Bianca had been helping Andrei write a love letter to someone else. Pietro felt like the stupidest boy in Florence. Then he laughed out loud, alone in his room, so loudly that Sara knocked on the door to ask whether he was all right. He replied to Andrei: “Beautiful. Best wishes to you both. And thank you.” Andrei replied with a question mark. Pietro never explained.

Pietro spent the next ten days preparing what he wanted to say to her, the way he had prepared the story for San Frediano: rewriting, cutting, looking for the right words. He wrote six versions in the black notebook. The first was three pages long. The sixth was three words. Then he thought words weren’t enough, and that a present was needed too. But not just any present. He asked Davide for help, who drew him a cover, and Bellini, who lent him the old bookbinding press from the workshop. In a week, working at night, Pietro hand-bound a little book with a green cloth cover, the same green as the “Firenze parla” notebook. Inside, on thick paper, he had copied by hand all the words of the “Dictionary of via Maggio”, the one they had begun together in July, after “abbraccioso”: “ribollitaio”, “domandoso”, “guardabene”, “tattigrafo”, “lunagrafo”, “minestrato”. And at the end, on the last page, a new word he had never told anyone, invented especially for her. Under the word he had written the definition. But the page was folded in two and tied with a red ribbon. On it was written: “To be opened only after I’ve told you”.

On Christmas Eve dinner was held, as every year, at Matei and Giulia’s, in Aldo’s old home above the trattoria, because it was the biggest. That year there were more than twenty of them. There were Ion and Doina, who had arrived from Sibiu the day before, on the usual twenty-six-hour train, with a suitcase full of cozonac, the Romanian Christmas cake, and hand-knitted woollen socks for everyone. There were Marco and Sara, Bellini, Karl, Davide with Rita, Efisio and Lucia, Guido, who for the first time in seventy-five years wasn’t spending Christmas Eve alone. There was Bianca, with her parents, whom Pietro barely knew and who looked at him with a new, suspicious attention, as if they knew something he didn’t. And there was Graziella, who that evening, for the first time Pietro could remember, cooked nothing. She sat at the table from beginning to end, in her blue Sunday dress, and let the others serve her. Karl had cooked everything, with Doina’s help. With each dish, Graziella tasted, closed her eyes and gave a mark. None went below eight. Karl, by the end, was so emotional he couldn’t eat a thing.

Before dessert came the exchange of presents. Doina had embroidered for Graziella a honey-coloured woollen shawl, with Transylvanian flowers along the edges, and told her, in her slow, careful Italian, that it was “for the sunsets”. Graziella didn’t understand. Doina explained that she had heard from Matei that in fifty-five years Graziella had never seen a sunset from any window but the one above the sink, and so she had made her a shawl for watching sunsets from the terrace in winter without catching cold. Graziella put it on at once and kept it on all evening. Ion, instead, gave Karl an old brass railwayman’s lantern with red glass, which he had used for thirty years on the Copșa Mică line. He said it was for people who work at night and get up before dawn, like railwaymen and cooks. “When you’re tired at five in the morning,” he told Karl, in an Italian that mixed words from 1990 with words of Guido’s, “light the lantern and think that somewhere an old Romanian railwayman is awake with you.” Karl held it in his hands for a long time without speaking. Then, that very evening, he hung it above the stove in the trattoria.

After dinner, while the grown-ups played tombola and Ion sang Romanian carols with Doina and Viola, Pietro asked Bianca to come up with him to the terrace in via della Chiesa, on the other side of the square. He said he wanted to show her the lights of Santo Spirito from above. Bianca looked at him and smiled, as if she had understood everything, and took her coat. They crossed the deserted square, under a cold, crystal-clear sky full of stars. They climbed the stairs to the fourth floor. On the terrace, next to Totò’s pot and the low wall where Viola had held up the “VOTE KARL” sign, you could see the whole city lit up: the bell tower of Santo Spirito, the dome of the Duomo, the distant hills of Arcetri, where they had seen the comet. Pietro had the green book in his coat pocket and his heart in his mouth. He had prepared six versions. He had chosen the last one, the three-word one. But when he opened his mouth, something completely different came out. “I have to tell you something,” he said. “I’ve been thinking about it for weeks.” Bianca leaned on the wall and looked at him. “For weeks?” she said. “I thought you’d never notice.”

Pietro remembered the rest of the conversation forever, but he never managed to write it in the black notebook, because every time he tried, the words seemed too small. Bianca told him she had been hoping he would speak before the year was over. He confessed that at Arcetri he had been afraid she liked Andrei. She laughed and said she had told him, “not in the way you think”, and that she had been sorry he hadn’t understood. He said he wished he had understood sooner, and that he was a bit ashamed. She told him not to be ashamed, that she was in no hurry, but that now he had to say it. And then Pietro said the three words of the sixth version, the ones he had written and crossed out and rewritten for ten days. “Ti voglio bene.” Then, afraid they weren’t enough, he added: “Not ‘like’. Really.” Bianca was silent for a moment. Then she took both his hands, which were frozen, and said: “I know. Me too.” And after a while, smiling: “And for once you didn’t ask a single question.” Below them, from Aldo’s home, came Ion’s voice singing “Florile dalbe”, and Viola’s laughter.

Then Pietro gave her the green book. Bianca leafed through it by the light of the street lamp in the square, page by page, laughing and moved at the same time, recognising every word, every evening, every interview. When she reached the last page, the one folded in two with the red ribbon, she read the words: “To be opened only after I’ve told you”. She looked at Pietro. “You’ve told me,” she said. She untied the ribbon and opened the page. A single word was written there, in Pietro’s neatest handwriting: “Bianchezza”. And below, the definition, as in a real dictionary: “Bianchezza, n.f.: the feeling of finally finding the right word. From the proper name Bianca plus the suffix -ezza, as in ‘bellezza’, ‘certezza’, ‘dolcezza’. Example: ‘When I met you, I felt a great bianchezza.’ A well-formed word. Waiting to be used by at least two people.” Bianca read it twice. Then she closed the book, held it to her chest and said, her voice a little broken: “You’re a bischero.” Pietro, who knew Florentine by now, knew it was the loveliest thing she could have said to him.

When they went back to Aldo’s home, hand in hand, everyone pretended not to notice, which was much worse than if they had noticed. Ion stopped singing in the middle of a verse. Doina elbowed Ion. Bianca’s parents exchanged a glance. Davide, from the corner, gave a thumbs-up. Guido said loudly “About time!”, and was hushed by Rita. And Viola, who had no intention of pretending, jumped off her chair, ran to them, hugged them both round the legs and shouted, in front of twenty people: “They’re abbracciosi! Both of them!” Bianca went as red as the ribbon on the book. Pietro wished he could disappear under the table. But Graziella, from her chair, was watching them with a smile Pietro had never seen on her, a slow, full smile, almost a girl’s. She beckoned him over. When Pietro bent down, she said in his ear, so that nobody could hear: “Your grandfather took a year of ribollite. You only took six months of words. You’re faster than he was.” Then, even more quietly: “But she’s more patient than I was.”

Later, while Ion and Doina were teaching everyone to dance a Romanian hora round the table, Bianca’s father took Pietro aside, by the window. He was a hydraulic engineer, tall and serious, who worked for the City Council and whom Pietro had seen only twice, always in passing. Pietro braced himself for the worst. Instead Bianca’s father told him a story. He said that he and Bianca’s mother had met at seventeen, at school, and that it had taken him two whole years to declare his love, because he was afraid of ruining the friendship. Two years. During which she, as she confessed to him much later, had feared he would never make up his mind. “Bianca takes after her mother in everything,” he said. “Patience and stubbornness. I was hoping she’d find someone who wouldn’t make her wait two years.” Then he shook Pietro’s hand, with an engineer’s grip. “Six months,” he said. “Not bad. But next time you have something important to tell her, don’t take six versions.” Pietro went red to the ears. He wondered how he knew about the six versions. Then he saw Davide, on the other side of the room, whistling and looking at the ceiling.

Graziella’s last service was on New Year’s Eve. The trattoria was fuller than it had ever been: there hadn’t been a free table for weeks, because the news had spread through the whole neighbourhood, and then the whole city, thanks to an article by Mancini titled “The last ribollita”. The regular customers came and the old ones too, some who hadn’t been seen for years. The mud angels of Florence came, with Efisio at their head. Dr Neri came, sat at the corner table and checked his watch every half hour, to make sure Graziella didn’t work more than six hours. Don Paolo came from San Leonardo. Lawyer Bardi came with his wife. Even Ferraris came from Milan, the man who had wanted to buy the recipe, with an enormous bunch of flowers and a card that said only: “Not the price, the conditions. With admiration.” Graziella cooked together with Karl, side by side, for the last time. But Pietro noticed that halfway through the evening his grandmother began to take a step back, then another, leaving Karl the central stove, then the ladle, then the orders. At eleven, Karl was cooking alone. And Graziella was watching him, leaning against the kitchen door, her arms folded.

At five to midnight, when the whole trattoria was on its feet, glasses in hand, ready for the countdown, Graziella went into the kitchen for the last time. Pietro followed her without being seen and stopped in the doorway. He saw her go to the window above the sink, where Aldo’s plant was, and pinch off a sprig of nepitella with her fingers. She put it in a yoghurt pot full of soil, which she had prepared that morning, and gave it to Karl. She told him it was that year’s cutting, as he had sworn on Ferragosto, and that from then on it was up to him, together with Viola, the keeper of the pot, to keep Aldo’s plant alive. Then she took off her apron. She folded it carefully, the way you fold a flag. And instead of putting it in the drawer, she hung it on the nail by the door, the one where for fifty years she had hung her market bag. She smoothed it with her hand. Then she took from the drawer the wooden spoon, the one worn down on one side, which had been her father Renzo’s before it was hers, and held it out to Karl. Karl took it with both hands, the way you take something sacred. He said nothing. There was no need. Outside, the room began to count: “Ten! Nine! Eight!”

When the room shouted “Happy New Year!”, Graziella came out of the kitchen without her apron, for the first time in fifty-five years. The applause lasted five minutes. People clapped, stamped their feet, tapped their spoons on their glasses. The mud angels sang. Guido cried without shame. Viola, in Matei’s arms, waved a streamer. Graziella stopped in the middle of the room, small, upright, in her blue dress with her hands empty, and for a moment she seemed not to know what to do with those hands without a ladle, without a plate, without a cloth. Then she did the thing she did best. She began to hug. One by one. Dr Neri, who checked his watch and said it was six hours and one minute. Don Paolo. Efisio. Ferraris, who stood stiff as a post and then melted. Bardi. Guido. Ion and Doina. Marco, for a long time. Pietro, for even longer. Bianca, who whispered something in her ear that made Graziella laugh. And last of all Karl, who had come out of the kitchen with the wooden spoon still in his hand and the new white apron Graziella had given him for Christmas, embroidered with: “Il cuoco”.

Karl made no speeches. He said only that the kitchen would reopen on the second of January, at five in the morning, as always. Then he went back into the kitchen, and ten minutes later, at half past midnight, he came out with a steaming bowl of ribollita and set it in front of Graziella, who had sat down at the corner table, the one by Aldo’s plant, with Bianca and Pietro. It was the first ribollita of 2030. The first from Karl’s kitchen. And the first, in fifty-five years, that Graziella ate as a customer. She tasted it in silence, watched by the whole room, waiting for the verdict with bated breath. Then she put down the spoon. “Sciocca,” she said. Karl went pale. Graziella let one second pass, two, three. Then she smiled. “The bread, I mean,” she said. “The way it should be. The rest is perfect.” The room erupted again. Then Graziella took a ten-euro note out of her purse and put it on the table. Karl protested that she didn’t have to pay, that it was her trattoria. Graziella shook her head. “Not any more,” she said. “Now it’s yours. And whoever comes in gets fed. But whoever can, pays.”

Later, when the trattoria had emptied and only they were left, sitting round the big table among the empty glasses and the streamers on the floor, Pietro asked his grandmother how she felt. Graziella thought for a long time, turning her glass between her fingers. Then she said she had thought she would be sad. That for weeks she had dreaded that evening, dreaded the moment she would take off her apron, dreaded feeling empty, useless, finished. But no. She said she was glad it had ended like this, with everyone around, with the kitchen in good hands, with Aldo’s plant safe. She said she felt a mixture of things: gratitude, relief, a little melancholy, and something she didn’t know how to name. A kind of lightness. Like when, after a whole day in the kitchen, you finally sit down and realise how tired your feet were only at the moment they stop hurting. Bianca, sitting next to Pietro with the green book on her knees, said softly: “Maybe it’s bianchezza.” Graziella looked at her without understanding. Pietro explained. Graziella laughed until she cried. “Then yes,” she said. “It really is bianchezza.”

Before going to bed, Graziella did one last thing. She went up to Aldo’s old home, where everyone was sleeping, and tiptoed into Viola’s room. The little girl was asleep with Assunta’s thimble on the bedside table and the streamer still clutched in her hand. Graziella switched on the little light in the corridor and looked at the door frame, with all the notches: Marco, Pietro, Viola, and that strange notch at heart height, “15 agosto. Ha capito”. She took the pencil from the pocket of her dress, where her apron used to be, and next to her grandchildren’s notches, much lower down, at the height of a ten-year-old girl, she drew a new line. Beside it she wrote: “Graziella, 1 January 2030. Starting again”. Pietro, who had followed her without being heard, watched her from the door. He asked her why so low. Graziella smiled. She said that day she felt as she had at ten, before the mud, before the trattoria, before everything. With her whole life ahead of her, and no hurry. Then she switched off the light and kissed him on the forehead. “Goodnight, il mi’ cittino,” she said. “Tomorrow we sleep late. Both of us.”
